question.question_text:
Baytree Island’s Council is concerned to retain a balance of skilled professional workers amongst the population, and monitors migrants in and migrants out on an annual basis. There is currently some concern about the trend, and the Chief Administration Officer was asked to prepare a statistical table for the next Council meeting, as shown below:
economically
total professionals other employed inactive in P M F P M F P M F P M F
2017 174 92 82 44 32 12 33 19 14 97 41 56
2016 154 83 71 45 32 13 24 14 10 85 37 48
2015 202 101 101 44 35 9 38 18 20 120 48 72
2014 201 107 94 55 40 15 36 21 15 110 46 64
2013 201 102 99 59 41 18 32 15 17 110 46 64 out P M F P M F P M F P M F
2017 159 94 65 65 49 16 32 22 10 62 23 39
2016 232 132 100 67 50 17 60 38 22 105 44 61
2015 260 136 124 68 49 19 66 37 29 126 50 76
2014 183 89 94 50 32 18 35 19 16 98 38 60
2013 165 80 85 51 32 19 35 16 19 79 32 47
Key: P=persons, M=males, F=females
In which year did the island have the greatest overall loss of professionals?

main_body.text: Baytree Island’s Council is concerned to retain a balance of skilled professional workers amongst the population, and monitors migrants in and migrants out on an annual basis. There is currently some concern about the trend, and the Chief Administration Officer was asked to prepare a statistical table for the next Council meeting, as shown below:

question.main_question: In which year did the island have the greatest overall loss of professionals?

blocks.text: Use the professionals' P column, since P counts all persons. Net loss equals professionals leaving minus professionals arriving. The losses for 2013–2017 are respectively 51−59 = −8, 50−55 = −5, 68−44 = 24, 67−45 = 22 and 65−44 = 21. The largest loss is 24 in 2015, so C is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: In 2013, 59 professionals arrive and 51 leave: a gain of 8 rather than a loss.

items.label: B
items.text: In 2014, 55 arrive and 50 leave, giving a net gain of 5.

items.label: D
items.text: The 2016 loss is 67−45 = 22, smaller than the loss of 24 in 2015.

items.label: E
items.text: The 2017 loss is 65−44 = 21, also smaller than the 2015 loss.

blocks.text: Read the visible upper segments using the complete display as a guide. The first hour digit has only its upper-right segment: 1. The second has both upper verticals but no top horizontal: 4. The minute tens has a top and upper-left segment but no upper-right segment; among valid minute tens this is 5. The time is therefore 14:5_, which rounds to 15:00, or 3 o'clock: C.

items.label: A
items.text: About 13:00 would require the hour to be 12 or 13, whose second digit has a top horizontal segment unlike the visible 4.

items.label: B
items.text: The display is in the last ten minutes of the 14th hour, so it rounds up to 15:00 rather than down to 14:00.

items.label: D
items.text: A time rounding to 16:00 would have an hour such as 15 or 16; those second hour digits have a top segment absent here.

items.label: E
items.text: A time near 17:00 likewise cannot have the displayed hour 14.

9 Shooting is not just positive for rural economies, but is also necessary for conservation efforts.
In various peripheral rural places in Britain, sport shooting related jobs are a mainstay of local
economies, often accounting for as much as a third of the labour market. However, since
humans disturbed the ecosystem by eradicating the top predators, destroying habitats and
introducing non-native species, we are also now responsible for reducing further damage –
conserving – by continuous management. This means shooting overpopulated species to
minimise the risks of disease and starvation, and dominant foreign species in order to conserve
weaker native ones. Additionally, the management of the environment for the purposes of sport
shooting can have very positive conservation effects; for example, many endangered birds of
prey now thrive on shooting estates.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?
A Wild flower numbers and bee populations have increased on shooting estates.
B Many animals that are shot are sold on to butchers and enter the food market.
C People from all over the world travel to Britain to engage in sport shooting.
D Many native species such as the red squirrel are at threat from foreign species.
E Re-introducing top predators such as wolves is a more effective means of conservation.

main_body.text:
Shooting is not just positive for rural economies, but is also necessary for conservation efforts.
In various peripheral rural places in Britain, sport shooting related jobs are a mainstay of local economies, often accounting for as much as a third of the labour market. However, since humans disturbed the ecosystem by eradicating the top predators, destroying habitats and introducing non-native species, we are also now responsible for reducing further damage –
conserving – by continuous management. This means shooting overpopulated species to minimise the risks of disease and starvation, and dominant foreign species in order to conserve weaker native ones. Additionally, the management of the environment for the purposes of sport shooting can have very positive conservation effects; for example, many endangered birds of prey now thrive on shooting estates.

question.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument maintains that shooting is necessary for conservation because humans have disrupted ecosystems by eliminating predators, introducing foreign species and damaging habitats. It presents shooting overpopulated or invasive animals as a way to manage these problems.

E challenges the necessity of shooting by proposing that reintroducing top predators is a more effective conservation method. If restoring predators can control animal populations more effectively, conservation may be achieved without relying on shooting as the necessary solution. This directly weakens the argument's claim of necessity, although it does not dispute shooting's possible economic benefits.

items.label: A
items.text: Increased wildflowers and bee populations on shooting estates would provide additional evidence that the management of these estates can benefit conservation.

items.label: B
items.text: Selling shot animals for food describes another use of the animals but does not establish that shooting is unnecessary or ineffective for conservation.

items.label: C
items.text: International visitors participating in sport shooting could contribute to rural economies, supporting the economic part of the argument rather than undermining its conservation claims.

items.label: D
items.text: Threats to native species from introduced foreign species support the argument's concern that such species require management to protect native populations.

10 Thousands of parents have recently been prosecuted by local education authorities for taking
their children out of school to go on holiday during term time. I took my daughter out of primary
school for a two-week holiday every year. The headmistress made no objection and said it
would give the other kids time to catch up with her! She was able to learn a foreign language
and spend some rewarding time with her French pen-pal. She eventually achieved top grades
at school and a degree in mathematics, so it obviously did her no harm! Parents, not
governments, know best how to raise children. This law is quite unnecessary.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?
A It is an appeal to tradition because it suggests that taking children on holiday in term time
used to be acceptable.
B It is based on authority as it uses the headmistress’s lack of objection in support.
C It assumes that because the daughter’s good grades were achieved after her foreign
holidays, they were the result of the holidays.
D It is based entirely on the one example of the daughter and generalises from that.
E It assumes that learning some French adequately compensated for the work the daughter
missed.

Thousands of parents have recently been prosecuted by local education authorities for taking their children out of school to go on holiday during term time. I took my daughter out of primary school for a two-week holiday every year. The headmistress made no objection and said it would give the other kids time to catch up with her! She was able to learn a foreign language and spend some rewarding time with her French pen-pal. She eventually achieved top grades at school and a degree in mathematics, so it obviously did her no harm! Parents, not governments, know best how to raise children. This law is quite unnecessary.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It is an appeal to tradition because it suggests that taking children on holiday in term time used to be acceptable.

options.label: B
options.text: It is based on authority as it uses the headmistress’s lack of objection in support.

options.label: C
options.text: It assumes that because the daughter’s good grades were achieved after her foreign holidays, they were the result of the holidays.

options.label: D
options.text: It is based entirely on the one example of the daughter and generalises from that.

options.label: E
options.text: It assumes that learning some French adequately compensated for the work the daughter missed.

main_body.text: Thousands of parents have recently been prosecuted by local education authorities for taking their children out of school to go on holiday during term time. I took my daughter out of primary school for a two-week holiday every year. The headmistress made no objection and said it would give the other kids time to catch up with her! She was able to learn a foreign language and spend some rewarding time with her French pen-pal. She eventually achieved top grades at school and a degree in mathematics, so it obviously did her no harm! Parents, not governments, know best how to raise children. This law is quite unnecessary.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The author argues that laws restricting term-time holidays are unnecessary, using the experience of one daughter who missed school for holidays yet subsequently achieved excellent academic results. However, the fact that one child experienced no apparent educational harm does not establish that term-time absences are harmless for children generally.

Different children may have different learning needs and may be affected differently by missing lessons. The argument therefore generalises from one favourable personal example to a broad policy conclusion. This is the flaw identified by D.

items.label: A
items.text: The author mentions past experience but does not claim that term-time holidays should be permitted simply because they were previously acceptable. The argument relies on the daughter's outcome.

items.label: B
items.text: The headmistress's approval supports the description of the individual case, but the wider conclusion is based primarily on the daughter's success rather than the headmistress's authority.

items.label: C
items.text: The author uses the daughter's good grades to suggest the holidays did not harm her education. The argument does not need to claim that the holidays caused those grades.

items.label: E
items.text: Learning French is presented as one benefit of the holidays, but the author also cites subsequent academic success. The conclusion does not depend specifically on French learning compensating for missed schoolwork.

main_body.text: Evidence suggests that children whose parents are married tend to fare better – financially, academically and socially – than children of unmarried parents. The government is therefore proposing a tax break for married couples, whereby married couples are reimbursed by approximately £150 per person per annum. This idea is flawed for several reasons. First, it punishes those whose partners have left them and broken up the marriage. Secondly, it punishes those who, through no fault of their own, have been unable to find a partner. Thirdly, it assumes that people in unhappy relationships will persevere in their unhappy state for something like £12.50 a month. This is patently absurd. Finally, it makes the bogus assumption that maintaining a poor marriage will be better for the children than separation.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The passage argues against the government's proposal to provide tax breaks to married couples. Although evidence suggests that children of married parents tend to fare better, the author identifies several problems with using financial incentives to encourage marriage: disadvantages for people whose relationships ended or who cannot find partners, the limited financial incentive for unhappy couples, and the unsupported assumption that remaining in an unhappy marriage benefits children.

These criticisms all support the overall judgement that the proposed tax-break policy is flawed. Therefore, E expresses the main conclusion.

items.label: A
items.text: The possibility that an unhappy relationship harms children is one reason used to criticise the policy, not the author's overall conclusion about the tax break.

items.label: B
items.text: The tendency for children of married parents to fare better is introduced as evidence motivating the government's proposal. It is not the conclusion the author seeks to establish.

items.label: C
items.text: The inadequacy of the financial incentive for unhappy couples is one supporting criticism, not the complete argument against the policy.

items.label: D
items.text: The policy's disadvantage to some single people is another reason for opposing it, but the argument also raises concerns about incentives and children's welfare.

blocks.text: Enough whole rolls must be bought to supply at least 54 m. Embossed needs 14 rolls of 4 m; its 25% discount gives 14×£50×0.75 = £525. The comparable totals are woodchip £550, vymura £567, anaglypta £576 and fabric effect £600. Embossed, D, is cheapest.

items.label: A
items.text: Woodchip needs 27 rolls. Five are free under every-fifth-roll-free, leaving 22×£25 = £550, £25 more than embossed.

items.label: B
items.text: Vymura needs 18 rolls: 18×£35×0.9 = £567 after its qualifying discount.

items.label: C
items.text: Anaglypta also needs 18 rolls, costing 18×£40×0.8 = £576 after discount.

15 The award of a Nobel Prize in economics, but not in psychology, sociology or anthropology,
seems to imply that economics is not a social science, but an exact one, like chemistry or
physics. Underpinning this idea is the thought that the human world operates like the physical
world. Economists themselves perpetuate this impression by dealing in hard quantitative data,
as opposed to observation and qualitative analysis. The defining feature of the natural sciences
is their consistent success in making predictions, but almost all economists failed to predict the
2008 financial crisis. The striking collapse of LTCM, a hedge fund set up by two economists
who were later awarded the Nobel Prize, further underscores the limits of economics to make
accurate forecasts.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?
A The Nobel Prize should not be awarded for economics.
B The human world is not part of the physical world.
C Economics is not a science like chemistry or physics.
D Economists cannot predict the behaviour of markets.
E Hard quantitative data has no role in economics.

main_body.text:
The award of a Nobel Prize in economics, but not in psychology, sociology or anthropology, seems to imply that economics is not a social science, but an exact one, like chemistry or physics. Underpinning this idea is the thought that the human world operates like the physical world. Economists themselves perpetuate this impression by dealing in hard quantitative data, as opposed to observation and qualitative analysis. The defining feature of the natural sciences is their consistent success in making predictions, but almost all economists failed to predict the
2008 financial crisis. The striking collapse of LTCM, a hedge fund set up by two economists who were later awarded the Nobel Prize, further underscores the limits of economics to make accurate forecasts.

question.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

blocks.text:
The passage distinguishes economics from natural sciences by emphasising the consistent predictive success attributed to sciences such as chemistry and physics. Although economics uses quantitative data and is sometimes presented as an exact science, the author points to economists' widespread failure to predict the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of a hedge fund established by prominent economists.

These examples challenge the claim that economics possesses the same forecasting reliability as the natural sciences. Therefore, C follows: economics is not a science in the same sense as chemistry or physics, particularly regarding consistent predictive success.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage questions the impression created by awarding a Nobel Prize in economics, but it does not conclude that the award itself should be abolished.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument challenges the idea that human affairs can be predicted as reliably as physical phenomena. It does not claim that human existence is separate from the physical world.

items.label: D
items.text: The failure to predict major events demonstrates limitations in economic forecasting, not that economists are incapable of making any accurate market predictions.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage notes economists' use of quantitative data but questions whether this makes economics an exact science. It does not claim that quantitative analysis is useless.

Mobile phone use and driving under the influence of alcohol are not the only examples of irresponsible driver behaviour. Tiredness when driving a vehicle is said to be responsible for
300 deaths per year. Astonishingly, almost half of male drivers and 22% of female drivers admit to having fallen asleep at the wheel. If we assume (and it seems reasonable to do so) that even more people are injured than killed as a result of accidents caused by tiredness, it is clear that tiredness while driving is a major road safety issue – and entirely preventable. question.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The passage argues that driving while dangerously tired is a preventable road safety risk and concludes that people should avoid driving when they have had insufficient sleep or rest to drive safely.

For this recommendation to work as a practical means of preventing accidents, drivers must be capable of recognising when their tiredness makes driving unsafe. If drivers cannot identify dangerous fatigue, they cannot reliably act on the instruction to avoid driving when insufficiently rested. Therefore, B is the underlying assumption linking the proposed precaution to the prevention of fatigue-related accidents.

items.label: A
items.text: The reported differences in falling asleep at the wheel do not establish that women are generally more careful. The argument does not require any explanation of those differences.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage identifies fatigue as a serious risk but does not compare its severity with mobile phone use. The recommendation does not depend on fatigue being more dangerous.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument recommends avoiding unsafe driving, but it does not require every professional long-distance driver to be able to avoid fatigue in all circumstances.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument does not depend on whether previous road safety campaigns have adequately emphasised tiredness. Its recommendation follows from the stated safety risk.

17 There has been a significant rise in the number of children with rickets. This has resulted from
the airless, indoor world we have created for ourselves. Rickets is caused by a deficiency of
vitamin D, which is produced in response to sunlight on the skin. Where children used to play
outside they mostly stay indoors immersed in virtual realities via various electronic
media. Instead of long summer evenings outdoors, we close the curtains to prevent sunlight
falling on our screens. The lure of technology is compounded by adult fears of the risks to

public spaces for open air activity. Curing this will require an awful lot more than vitamin pills.

C The incidence of rickets is confined to a few hundred cases a year.
D In the 19th century, when the incidence of rickets was much higher, terrible air pollution
and smog affected the large population of city dwellers.
E Many people can’t afford or be relied on to take vitamin D supplements.

main_body.text: There has been a significant rise in the number of children with rickets. This has resulted from the airless, indoor world we have created for ourselves. Rickets is caused by a deficiency of vitamin D, which is produced in response to sunlight on the skin. Where children used to play outside they mostly stay indoors immersed in virtual realities via various electronic media. Instead of long summer evenings outdoors, we close the curtains to prevent sunlight falling on our screens. The lure of technology is compounded by adult fears of the risks to children if they are left to roam free in the outside world; in any case there are fewer accessible public spaces for open air activity. Curing this will require an awful lot more than vitamin pills.

question.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument attributes rising cases of rickets mainly to children spending more time indoors, where they receive less sunlight and consequently produce less vitamin D. It concludes that addressing the problem requires broader changes than simply providing vitamin supplements.

B weakens this explanation by stating that diet has a much greater influence on vitamin D intake than sunlight. If dietary factors are substantially more important, reduced outdoor activity may be less significant as the cause of vitamin D deficiency than the passage suggests. This challenges the argument's emphasis on an indoor lifestyle as the central explanation for increasing rickets cases.

items.label: A
items.text: An increase in parkland could challenge the claim that outdoor spaces are becoming less available, but it does not establish that children actually spend more time outdoors or receive enough sunlight.

items.label: C
items.text: A few hundred annual cases could still represent a significant increase from an earlier level. The absolute number does not directly challenge the proposed cause.

items.label: D
items.text: Historical air pollution and smog provide a possible explanation for earlier cases of rickets, but they do not establish that today's reduced outdoor activity is unrelated to vitamin D deficiency.

items.label: E
items.text: Difficulty accessing or consistently taking vitamin supplements would make supplementation a less reliable solution, supporting rather than weakening the argument that more than vitamin pills may be needed.

Five girls are collecting shells on a beach. They are putting them in buckets that each hold 24
shells. At the end of the collecting time, they are going to ensure that they all have the same
number of shells. Four of them are only two short of filling their bucket, but the youngest one is
lagging behind with her total. Each of the others give her three shells from their buckets in
order to equalise the numbers collected.
How many shells did the youngest girl collect for herself?

main_body.text: Five girls are collecting shells on a beach. They are putting them in buckets that each hold 24 shells. At the end of the collecting time, they are going to ensure that they all have the same number of shells. Four of them are only two short of filling their bucket, but the youngest one is lagging behind with her total. Each of the others give her three shells from their buckets in order to equalise the numbers collected.

question.main_question: How many shells did the youngest girl collect for herself?

blocks.text:
Four girls each collected 24 − 2 = 22 shells. Each then gives 3 shells to the youngest girl, leaving each of the four with 22 − 3 = 19 shells.

To make all five totals equal, the youngest girl must also finish with 19 shells. She receives 4 × 3 = 12 shells from the others, so the number she originally collected is 19 − 12 = 7. Therefore, B is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: If the youngest girl originally had 4 shells, receiving 12 more would leave her with 16, which is 3 fewer than each other girl.

items.label: C
items.text: Starting with 10 shells would give the youngest girl 22 after the transfers, exceeding the others' final totals of 19.

items.label: D
items.text: Starting with 12 shells would produce a final total of 24, which is 5 more than each other girl retains.

items.label: E
items.text: 19 is the number of shells each girl must have after redistribution, not the youngest girl's original collection. Starting with 19 would leave her with 31 after receiving the additional shells.

21 When mobile phones first became relatively inexpensive many parents bought them for their
teenage children on the grounds that having access to a phone would keep them safe. High
profile cases of abduction at the time underscored the need to improve safety for young
people. But today mobile phones invariably have access to the internet, which has made young
people vulnerable to stalking and cyberbullying. Since the stated case for buying teenagers
mobile phones was to keep them safe, we should now restrict their access to them.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?
A The incidence of cyberbullying and stalking does not undermine the respects in which
mobile phones keep teenagers safe.
B If you restrict young people’s access to mobile phones they will continue to bully one
another on other devices.
C Access to mobile phones has not stopped teenagers from being attacked while out alone
at night.
D The majority of teenagers are not affected by the problems of stalking and cyberbullying.
E It ignores the fact that there are other ways of keeping children safe.

question.question_text:
When mobile phones first became relatively inexpensive many parents bought them for their teenage children on the grounds that having access to a phone would keep them safe. High profile cases of abduction at the time underscored the need to improve safety for young people. But today mobile phones invariably have access to the internet, which has made young people vulnerable to stalking and cyberbullying. Since the stated case for buying teenagers mobile phones was to keep them safe, we should now restrict their access to them.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The incidence of cyberbullying and stalking does not undermine the respects in which mobile phones keep teenagers safe.

options.label: B
options.text: If you restrict young people’s access to mobile phones they will continue to bully one another on other devices.

options.label: C
options.text: Access to mobile phones has not stopped teenagers from being attacked while out alone at night.

options.label: D
options.text: The majority of teenagers are not affected by the problems of stalking and cyberbullying.

options.label: E
options.text: It ignores the fact that there are other ways of keeping children safe.

main_body.text: When mobile phones first became relatively inexpensive many parents bought them for their teenage children on the grounds that having access to a phone would keep them safe. High profile cases of abduction at the time underscored the need to improve safety for young people. But today mobile phones invariably have access to the internet, which has made young people vulnerable to stalking and cyberbullying. Since the stated case for buying teenagers mobile phones was to keep them safe, we should now restrict their access to them.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The original justification for giving teenagers mobile phones was that they could improve safety, particularly in situations such as abduction. The argument now recommends restricting phones because internet access exposes teenagers to stalking and cyberbullying.

However, introducing new risks does not establish that the original safety benefits have disappeared. Mobile phones could still protect teenagers in certain situations while exposing them to different dangers. The argument fails to consider both effects before recommending restrictions. Therefore, A identifies the flaw.

items.label: B
items.text: Bullying through other devices might limit the effectiveness of restricting phones, but this is a separate practical objection. The central flaw is the failure to consider the phones' continuing safety benefits.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage does not claim that phones prevent every attack. Their failure to prevent some incidents would not establish that they provide no protection in other situations.

items.label: D
items.text: Even if most teenagers were unaffected by stalking or cyberbullying, those risks could still be significant. The flaw concerns overlooking existing benefits, not the precise proportion affected.

items.label: E
items.text: Alternative ways of protecting children might exist, but the argument does not depend on phones being the only safety measure. The problem is that their original benefits are disregarded.

question.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The supermarket scheme establishes that customers spending £40 a week receive vouchers. The argument then concludes that spending only £15 means receiving no vouchers. However, the stated rule guarantees vouchers to customers meeting the threshold without explicitly ruling out vouchers for other customers.

B follows the same reasoning: completing a main course guarantees dessert, but the argument concludes that someone who has not completed it will receive no dessert. Both arguments incorrectly infer that failing a stated sufficient condition makes the outcome impossible. Therefore, B is the closest parallel.

items.label: A
items.text: Introducing new gym customers satisfies the stated condition for receiving a discount. The conclusion applies the rule directly rather than denying the benefit because the condition is absent.

items.label: C
items.text: Being 30 satisfies the stated age requirement of 18–30 inclusive. The conclusion correctly applies the eligibility rule to someone within that range.

items.label: D
items.text: An income of £9000 satisfies the stated requirement of earning below £10000. The conclusion follows from meeting the condition rather than failing it.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument treats experience as necessary for appreciating good wine, then draws a conclusion about preferring poor wine. That additional preference is not established by the condition.

question.main_question: Which one of the following illustrates the principle used in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument condemns house-buying television programmes because they display attractive properties that many viewers cannot afford. Rather than merely generating interest, these programmes are claimed to create envy and feelings of worthlessness through comparison with unattainable lifestyles.

E illustrates the same principle: magazines displaying seemingly perfect people can encourage harmful comparisons with unrealistic ideals, producing dissatisfaction and potentially damaging consequences. Both arguments criticise media content for encouraging people to compare themselves unfavourably with idealised images.

items.label: A
items.text: This describes the housing circumstances of viewers but does not establish that watching attractive properties causes envy or feelings of inadequacy.

items.label: B
items.text: This presents exposure to desirable lifestyles as potentially motivating positive action. The original argument instead emphasises the harmful psychological effects of such comparisons.

items.label: C
items.text: This contrasts the public's perception of celebrity life with celebrities' actual anxieties. It does not identify harmful self-comparison among people viewing that lifestyle.

items.label: D
items.text: This compares the financial merits of renting and buying property. Its reasoning concerns housing costs, not the emotional harm caused by idealised media representations.

27 Long-term unemployment is a big problem for the UK, both for the government and for the
individual. The solution is unlikely to be one the government wishes to consider: invest money
in improving the skills of job centre staff. Some people argue that providing welfare benefits
makes unemployed people less motivated to find work. Other people, mostly outside the
government, think that not enough is done to provide the help needed to get people into work.
Neither side is right. Unemployed people are all different: some really want to work and would
do so if they had help; others are content to live on benefits. We have to steer away from one-
size-fits-all solutions and tailor the approach to the individual. But this needs much higher levels
of skilled staff than job centres currently have.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?
A Long-term unemployment is one of the biggest problems facing the UK.
B Unemployed people vary in their motivation to work.
C One-size-fits-all solutions tend to be cheaper than tailored approaches.
D The way to reduce unemployment is to spend on skilled staff in job centres.
E Welfare benefits provide a disincentive to work.

main_body.text:
Long-term unemployment is a big problem for the UK, both for the government and for the individual. The solution is unlikely to be one the government wishes to consider: invest money in improving the skills of job centre staff. Some people argue that providing welfare benefits makes unemployed people less motivated to find work. Other people, mostly outside the government, think that not enough is done to provide the help needed to get people into work.
Neither side is right. Unemployed people are all different: some really want to work and would do so if they had help; others are content to live on benefits. We have to steer away from one-
size-fits-all solutions and tailor the approach to the individual. But this needs much higher levels of skilled staff than job centres currently have.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument identifies long-term unemployment as a problem requiring different responses for different individuals. Some unemployed people want to work but need assistance, while others have less motivation to seek employment.

Because these differences make uniform policies inadequate, effective employment support requires individually tailored approaches. The author argues that implementing such approaches depends on having more highly skilled job-centre staff. Therefore, the principal recommendation is to invest in improving staff skills, as expressed in D.

items.label: A
items.text: Long-term unemployment is introduced as a serious problem, but the passage's main purpose is to recommend a particular solution rather than establish its relative importance.

items.label: B
items.text: Differences in motivation among unemployed people provide evidence for using tailored support. They are a supporting premise, not the policy conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage suggests tailored approaches require more skilled staff, but it does not compare their total costs with uniform approaches or claim that cheaper solutions should be preferred.

items.label: E
items.text: The possible disincentive created by welfare benefits is presented as one side of a debate that the author considers inadequate. It is not the author's main conclusion.

C Students were unjustified in complaining about the lack of computers.
D Students’ educational achievement is improved by using computers.
E Library use will necessarily increase if more computers are provided.

Amongst books borrowed, rates of late return or loss of books also increased by 10%. On the other hand, student use of computers in the library increased by 25%. This finding was reinforced by frequent complaints from students that there were no computers available when they needed to use them. question.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the librarian’s reasoning?

blocks.text:
The librarian observes that book borrowing has declined while computer use has increased, accompanied by complaints about insufficient computer availability. She responds by removing books and spending the library's entire available budget on additional computers.

This decision assumes that the library should adapt its resources to students' demonstrated preferences rather than attempt to influence those preferences or preserve existing resources for other purposes. Without that principle, increased computer demand would not automatically justify reallocating resources away from books. Therefore, A is the underlying assumption.

items.label: B
items.text: Declining library borrowing does not necessarily mean students are reading less, since they might obtain books elsewhere. The decision to provide more computers does not require assuming an overall decline in reading.

items.label: C
items.text: The librarian treats complaints about unavailable computers as evidence of demand. Assuming those complaints were unjustified would weaken rather than support her response.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument does not establish or require that computers improve educational achievement. It bases resource allocation on usage and expressed demand.

items.label: E
items.text: The librarian can respond to existing demand without assuming that providing more computers will necessarily increase total library usage.

main_body.text:
Recently, packets of Amblers crisps have had ‘money-off’ coupons inside them. Some coupons are worth 9p, some are worth 14p and some are worth 20p.
George has been collecting these coupons. He has more 14p coupons than 9p coupons, and more 9p coupons than 20p coupons. The total value of all of his coupons is exactly £1.50.

question.main_question: How many coupons has George collected?

blocks.text:
Let a, b and c be the numbers of 9p, 14p and 20p coupons. Their total value is 150p, so 9a + 14b + 20c = 150, with b > a > c.

Since the total is even, a must be even. Also, b ≥ a + 1, so 9a + 14(a + 1) ≤ 150, restricting a to 2 or 4. If a = 4, then 7b + 10c = 57, requiring b to end in 1, which is incompatible with b > 4 and the total value. Thus a = 2. The equation becomes 7b + 10c = 66, giving b = 8 and c = 1.

The counts satisfy 8 > 2 > 1, and the value is 8(14) + 2(9) + 1(20) = 150p. Total coupons = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. Therefore, C is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: With 9 coupons, the value equation permits counts of 0 nine-penny, 5 fourteen-penny and 4 twenty-penny coupons, but these violate the required ordering.

items.label: B
items.text: With 10 coupons, the compatible value counts are 4 nine-penny, 1 fourteen-penny and 5 twenty-penny coupons. The fourteen-penny count is not the largest.

items.label: D
items.text: With 12 coupons, the value equation gives 6 nine-penny, 4 fourteen-penny and 2 twenty-penny coupons. This violates b > a.

items.label: E
items.text: With 13 coupons, the value equation gives 10 nine-penny, 0 fourteen-penny and 3 twenty-penny coupons, contradicting the required ordering.

The current advice from the NHS in the UK is to eat five portions of fruit and vegetables a day.
However, a recent study suggested that at least seven portions are needed to maximise health.
Given that less than a third of adults in the UK, and even fewer children, currently meet the five-a-day target, there is little to be gained from changing the NHS advice to a higher number.
A higher target might even be counter-productive, as evidence shows that a change in diet is best sustained when the change is made slowly and incrementally.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The passage acknowledges research suggesting that seven daily portions of fruit and vegetables maximise health, but argues against raising the existing five-portion target. Fewer than a third of UK adults, and even fewer children, currently meet the lower target. Furthermore, the passage states that dietary changes are sustained more successfully when introduced gradually.

These considerations suggest that increasing the official target could be ineffective or counterproductive. Therefore, C expresses the main conclusion: the current guidance should be maintained rather than increased.

items.label: A
items.text: The research suggests seven portions may maximise health, not that consuming fewer than seven necessarily prevents someone from being healthy.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage states that fewer than a third meet the current target, but it does not establish that everyone else deliberately ignores the guidance. Failure to meet a target does not necessarily indicate disregard.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument suggests that raising the target may be counterproductive under current circumstances. It does not establish that all ambitious dietary targets are inherently unrealistic.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage acknowledges recent research but argues that practical considerations favour retaining existing advice. It does not establish that the current guidance failed to consider the research.

main_body.text: Welfare benefits create a culture of dependency and an unproductive workforce. There are people who stay on welfare benefits for years and never look for employment. Two years ago the government introduced tougher restrictions on the eligibility to receive benefits and the number of recipients has now fallen by 20%. The government should therefore toughen these restrictions even more to further reduce the number of welfare claimants.

question.main_question: Which one of the following identifies the flaw in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument notes that welfare restrictions became tougher two years ago and that the number of benefit recipients subsequently fell by 20%. It then recommends further restrictions, treating the reduction as evidence that the policy worked and that additional restrictions will produce further reductions.

However, the sequence of events does not establish that the restrictions caused the entire decline. Other factors could have contributed to the reduction in recipient numbers. Without establishing the actual cause, the argument cannot reliably predict that stricter rules will produce the desired result. Therefore, C identifies the flaw.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage claims that some people remain on benefits without seeking employment, but it does not require assuming that every recipient is content with this situation.

items.label: B
items.text: The language may suggest criticism of benefit recipients, but the decisive reasoning flaw concerns attributing the decline in recipient numbers to the restrictions without excluding other causes.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument associates long-term welfare dependency with an unproductive workforce, but its policy inference specifically depends on the unexplained relationship between restrictions and reduced recipient numbers.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage does not establish that every recipient is personally responsible for requiring benefits. Nevertheless, the specific failure in the proposed policy argument is its unsupported causal inference.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The passage acknowledges Shakespeare's reputation and linguistic skill but questions whether these qualities alone explain his greatness, especially since many plays lack substantial plot or character development.

It proposes that his exceptional status instead derives chiefly from a small group of works: the four great tragedies. These plays are distinguished by their exploration of fundamental aspects of human existence, which enables them to affect audiences deeply. Therefore, D expresses the main conclusion: Shakespeare's greatness derives from a small number of his plays, particularly the great tragedies.

items.label: A
items.text: The enduring appeal of Shakespeare's treatment of appearances and reality is acknowledged as a characteristic of his writing, but the author argues that another feature better explains his greatness.

items.label: B
items.text: The apparent agreement about Shakespeare's greatness establishes the issue that the passage seeks to explain. It is the starting point rather than the conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: The emotional and intellectual impact of Shakespeare's tragedies explains why these particular plays account for his greatness. It is supporting reasoning rather than the complete conclusion.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage notes limited development of plot and character in many plays but does not conclude that these limitations have no effect on Shakespeare's reputation.

main_body.text:
There is an automatic photograph booth in my local shopping centre. It takes exactly 2 minutes from the time that the money is inserted for the photographs to be taken, then the developed photographs appear 4 minutes later.
Money may only be inserted when the green light is on. This light goes out immediately after money is inserted, and comes back on again exactly 3 minutes later.
This morning, I arrived at the booth just as it was being switched on, and I was sixth in the queue. The first person inserted their money immediately, and the rest of us all inserted our money as soon as we were allowed to.

question.main_question: How long after I arrived at the booth did I insert my money?

blocks.text:
The green light returns exactly 3 minutes after money is inserted, so consecutive customers can pay at 3-minute intervals. The first person inserts money immediately upon the booth opening, at 0 minutes.

As sixth in the queue, the narrator must wait for five earlier customers to insert their money. Their payment times are 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12 minutes. The narrator can therefore insert money at 5 × 3 = 15 minutes after arrival. The photograph-taking and development times do not change the stated payment interval. Therefore, A is correct.

items.label: B
items.text: 18 minutes is when the seventh customer could insert money. The narrator is sixth and therefore pays at 15 minutes.

items.label: C
items.text: 21 minutes corresponds to the eighth payment opportunity, two positions after the narrator's.

items.label: D
items.text: 25 minutes is not one of the permitted payment times, which occur at multiples of 3 minutes from the booth opening.

items.label: E
items.text: 30 minutes corresponds to the eleventh payment opportunity, five places later than the narrator's position.

main_body.text: The diagram below shows part of a map of Ruralia.

A group of students are on an expedition and must meet their teacher at Longwood, grid reference 787634. Unfortunately, they have been given a version of the map with the numbers missing from the gridlines, and the place names have been omitted too. They have a list of grid references for some places on the map, and are trying to work out which point to head for in order to be sure of meeting their teacher.

They have a set of instructions showing how the grid references work:
The grid reference of point P is 172427. Go to vertical line to the west of the point, read the number 17. Estimate how many tenths across the square the point appears at, hence 172. Go to horizontal line to the south of point P, read the number 42, estimate how many tenths up the square the point is, hence 427. This gives 172427 as the complete grid reference number.
Here is the list of the grid references / place names the students have been given.

question.main_question: Using this information to help you, which of the places marked on the map is Longwood?

blocks.text: Use both whole-square position and tenths within a square. Hilltop (763613) fixes the low-left point at easting 76.3, northing 61.3; the rest of the pattern then locates the grid. Longwood is 78.7 east and 63.4 north. The point W lies about seven tenths across the 78 square and four tenths above line 63, so W, B, is Longwood.

items.label: A
items.text: V is around 77.7/63.4: it has the correct northing but lies one whole square west of Longwood.

items.label: C
items.text: X is approximately 79.2/62.6, matching High Moor rather than Longwood.

items.label: D
items.text: Y is approximately 78.1/61.4, matching Riverside and lying much farther south.

items.label: E
items.text: Z is approximately 80.4/61.3, matching Sunnybank, east and south of Longwood.

39 Modern aeroplanes are for the most part ‘flown’ by autoflight computers. These computers can
take over when the plane is just 30 metres off the ground, maintain whatever speed and height
is tapped into the flight management system, and land the aircraft automatically. But when
autoflight computers experience situations they haven’t been programmed to handle – sudden
structural damage to the aircraft, or extreme weather – they can throw back responsibility to the
pilot, who may become confused over the level of control they have. The confusion is made
worse by flight deck computers overloading pilots with a blizzard of alerts. This is when crashes
are most likely to happen.
Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?
A Developing autoflight computers further to allow pilotless planes is likely to be safer than
the current arrangement.
B Automated systems can be refined to the extent that air crashes will not happen.
C The combination of computer and human control over an aircraft is unsafe in most
situations.
D Autoflight computers can be controlled as easily from the ground as from inside the plane.
E Human error in entering data into autoflight computers will always pose a risk.

main_body.text: Modern aeroplanes are for the most part ‘flown’ by autoflight computers. These computers can take over when the plane is just 30 metres off the ground, maintain whatever speed and height is tapped into the flight management system, and land the aircraft automatically. But when autoflight computers experience situations they haven’t been programmed to handle – sudden structural damage to the aircraft, or extreme weather – they can throw back responsibility to the pilot, who may become confused over the level of control they have. The confusion is made worse by flight deck computers overloading pilots with a blizzard of alerts. This is when crashes are most likely to happen.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?

blocks.text:
The passage identifies a particular danger in the current arrangement: when autoflight computers encounter unexpected situations, they may transfer control to pilots who are confused about their responsibilities and overwhelmed by alerts. Crashes are described as most likely during this breakdown in coordination.

A draws the inference that further development towards fully pilotless aircraft could reduce this danger by removing the problematic transfer between automated and human control. It is a prediction rather than a guarantee of safety, but it most directly follows from the identified weakness of the current combined system.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage identifies situations that existing systems cannot handle, but it provides no basis for claiming that further automation could eliminate every possible cause of an aircraft crash.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage locates the greatest danger in exceptional situations involving failed coordination. It does not claim that combining human and computer control is unsafe in most ordinary situations.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage discusses onboard flight computers and pilots but provides no information about controlling aircraft remotely from the ground.

items.label: E
items.text: The identified danger concerns unexpected situations, unclear control responsibilities and excessive alerts. The passage does not attribute crashes to incorrectly entered data or establish that such errors will always occur.

40 Children spend far too long in schools analysing poems when they should simply be learning to
enjoy them. Thankfully, a new approach requires that, instead of focusing on analysing
technical aspects of writing such as the writer’s use of imagery or alliteration, children will be
required simply to learn poems so that they can recite them by heart. This makes good sense.
What is the use of learning how to analyse literature if you have no appreciation of its actual
value? If they then become interested in it enough to study it at A level or at university, that can
be when they learn to analyse in detail the author’s craft.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?
A Analysing the writer’s craft could enhance the appreciation of the poem.
B Children are not currently required to learn poems off by heart.
C English will continue to be a subject available for study at A level or university.
D For something to be classed as poetry it must include either alliteration or imagery.
E Learning a poem off by heart will enable you to appreciate it more.

main_body.text:
Children spend far too long in schools analysing poems when they should simply be learning to enjoy them. Thankfully, a new approach requires that, instead of focusing on analysing technical aspects of writing such as the writer’s use of imagery or alliteration, children will be required simply to learn poems so that they can recite them by heart. This makes good sense.
What is the use of learning how to analyse literature if you have no appreciation of its actual value? If they then become interested in it enough to study it at A level or at university, that can be when they learn to analyse in detail the author’s craft.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument recommends replacing detailed literary analysis with memorisation and recitation because it believes children should develop an appreciation of poetry before studying its technical features.

For memorisation to be a suitable replacement, learning poems by heart must help children appreciate them. Otherwise, removing detailed analysis in favour of recitation would not necessarily achieve the objective of making poetry more enjoyable or valuable to students. Therefore, E is the underlying assumption linking the proposed teaching method to its intended benefit.

items.label: A
items.text: The possibility that literary analysis improves appreciation could favour retaining analysis. The argument does not require this benefit to exist before recommending memorisation.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage contrasts an existing emphasis on analysis with a new requirement to memorise poems, but the argument does not depend on proving that no children currently memorise poetry.

items.label: C
items.text: The availability of advanced literary study is mentioned as a possible later stage. The recommendation to develop appreciation first does not depend on the continued existence of every particular qualification.

items.label: D
items.text: Imagery and alliteration are examples of techniques studied in literary analysis. The argument does not require either technique to be present in every poem.

people with internships or work experience placements.

main_body.text:
The financial circumstances of many young people make it difficult for them to forego paid employment for an extended period in order to undertake unpaid internships or work experience placements. In many industries, it is unlikely that a young person will gain entry-
level paid employment unless he or she has held one of these temporary unpaid positions.
Therefore, the current system of unpaid internships creates an unfair advantage for individuals from more affluent backgrounds.

question.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument claims that unpaid internships unfairly favour wealthier young people because entry-level jobs often require experience that less affluent applicants cannot afford to obtain through extended periods of unpaid work.

C weakens this reasoning by establishing that internships vary considerably in duration, with some lasting only one or two days. Short placements may not require applicants to sacrifice paid employment for an extended period, reducing the force of the financial barrier described. This does not eliminate all inequality, but it challenges the assumption that obtaining relevant unpaid experience necessarily requires a prolonged financial sacrifice.

items.label: A
items.text: The opportunity to obtain useful references explains why internships can be valuable for employment. It does not weaken the concern that some applicants cannot afford to undertake them.

items.label: B
items.text: Concentrating opportunities in expensive or distant locations could create additional accessibility barriers rather than undermine the argument about unequal opportunities.

items.label: D
items.text: Some interns repeatedly failing to obtain paid work raises doubts about the effectiveness of internships, but it does not demonstrate that poorer applicants have equal access to them.

items.label: E
items.text: Programmes helping applicants find internships may improve access to vacancies, but they do not necessarily remove the financial difficulty of working without pay.

main_body.text:
In the main draw of a lottery, six of the balls (which are numbered from 1 to 49) are selected at random, then the numbers chosen are rearranged and displayed in ascending numerical order.
For instance: 3 17 20 29 34 45
In one draw recently, I noticed that the six numbers were made up of a total of ten digits, all different. The lowest number on this occasion was 1 and the highest number was 49, so the range of the six numbers was 48, the greatest possible range for the lottery main draw.

question.main_question: What is the smallest possible range when the six numbers in the main draw of the lottery have a total of ten digits, all different?

blocks.text:
Six numbers containing ten distinct digits must consist of two single-digit and four two-digit numbers. Because all ten digits are different, the four two-digit numbers must use distinct tens digits. Within the lottery's range of 1–49, those tens digits must be 1, 2, 3 and 4. Therefore, the largest number is at least 40.

The two distinct single-digit numbers must include one no greater than 8, so the smallest number is at most 8. Hence the range cannot be less than 40 − 8 = 32.

This minimum is achievable with 8, 9, 15, 26, 37 and 40. Their ten digits are all different, and the range is 40 − 8 = 32. Therefore, E is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: A range of 21 is smaller than the proven minimum of 32, which follows from the necessary presence of a number at least 40 and another at most 8.

items.label: B
items.text: A range of 23 cannot accommodate the required four distinct two-digit tens digits and two distinct single-digit numbers.

items.label: C
items.text: A range of 27 is below the minimum separation of 32 between the largest and smallest numbers.

items.label: D
items.text: 31 is one less than the theoretical minimum. The required largest number is at least 40 and the smallest is at most 8, giving a difference of at least 32.

45 Charities address the negative effects of market economies, which apportion goods to people
based on their ability to pay as opposed to their needs. The work of charities conceals the true
impact of the market system and, worse, leaves the market in place to produce further negative
outcomes. Charities therefore effectively perpetuate the problems the market system
creates. Since it is immoral to support a practice that perpetuates the very problems it is
supposed to resolve, giving to charity cannot be morally justified. After all, if the effects of a
system are morally wrong, then it is immoral to sustain that system.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?
A Charity does not address the cause of the problem.
B Charitable giving is necessary because of the market system.
C Charities perpetuate the negative effects of market economies.
D Giving to charity is immoral.
E Charities conceal the negative effects of the operation of the market.

The work of charities conceals the true impact of the market system and, worse, leaves the market in place to produce further negative outcomes. Charities therefore effectively perpetuate the problems the market system creates. question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument claims that charities relieve the negative consequences of market economies without correcting the underlying system responsible for those consequences. By concealing the system's harmful effects and allowing it to continue, charities are said to perpetuate the very problems they seek to solve.

The author then applies a moral principle: supporting a system that perpetuates harmful outcomes is immoral. Since charitable giving allegedly sustains such a system, the author concludes that giving to charity cannot be morally justified. Therefore, D expresses the main conclusion.

items.label: A
items.text: The claim that charity does not address the underlying cause is part of the argument explaining why charitable activity allegedly perpetuates problems. It is not the final moral conclusion.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage connects the existence of charities to problems created by market economies, but it does not conclude that charitable giving is necessary or desirable.

items.label: C
items.text: The alleged perpetuation of market-related harms is an intermediate conclusion used to justify the broader judgement about the morality of charitable giving.

items.label: E
items.text: The claim that charities conceal the negative consequences of the market is supporting evidence for the argument that they sustain the system.

main_body.text: You can only grasp the true meaning of Pushkin’s poetry if you can read it in its original Russian form. Your doctoral thesis on Pushkin’s work shows acute insight so I can tell you have a mastery of the Russian language.

question.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The original argument states that understanding the true meaning of Pushkin's poetry requires being able to read the original Russian. It then treats the doctoral thesis's acute insight as evidence that the writer possesses this understanding and concludes that the writer must know Russian.

D follows the same structure: a pedestrian-only high street requires a bypass, and the town has pedestrian-only shopping, so the argument concludes that the bypass must exist. Both infer a necessary condition from the presence of an outcome that supposedly requires it.

items.label: A
items.text: A clear sky is presented as necessary for astronomy, but the argument treats having a clear sky as sufficient to guarantee stargazing. This reverses the direction of the original reasoning.

items.label: B
items.text: Putting the dustbin out before 8 a.m. is stated as necessary for collection, but the argument incorrectly treats satisfying that requirement as sufficient to guarantee collection.

items.label: C
items.text: The Mensa argument infers the absence of a required qualification from non-membership. Failure to obtain membership does not establish that the IQ requirement was not met.

items.label: E
items.text: Having 45 flying hours is required before taking the test, and having only 18 hours establishes that this requirement is unmet. It reasons from the absence of a necessary condition, rather than inferring its presence from an observed outcome.

Inmates from an open prison have worked night-shifts on the main line from London to
Glasgow. This is the same line where a train left the tracks earlier this year, killing one person

cheap labour. This is unacceptable, not just for safety reasons – important as they are – but

C Rehabilitation should be for the prisoner’s benefit, not the employer’s.
D Prisoners who are given work should not take jobs away from other workers.
E Maintenance of public services should be in the hands of skilled professionals only.

main_body.text:
It has emerged that prisoners have helped to maintain one of Britain’s busiest railway lines.
Inmates from an open prison have worked night-shifts on the main line from London to Glasgow. This is the same line where a train left the tracks earlier this year, killing one person and injuring several others. It is all very well to have offenders being rehabilitated through work, but what appears to be happening here is that rail contractors are cynically using prisoners as cheap labour. This is unacceptable, not just for safety reasons – important as they are – but because ultimately it is an infringement of workers’ rights. If these prisoners are being paid less, or treated differently from regular workers, the practice must stop once and for all.

question.main_question: Which one of the following expresses the general principle that underlies the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument accepts that prisoners may benefit from rehabilitation through work but condemns using them as cheap labour if this means they receive lower pay or worse treatment than ordinary workers. The objection is therefore not to prisoners working, but to their labour being valued differently merely because of their prisoner status.

A expresses the general principle underlying this criticism: work should receive equivalent value and treatment regardless of who performs it. This explains why unequal treatment of prisoners and regular workers would make the arrangement unacceptable.

items.label: B
items.text: Public safety is mentioned as a concern, but the argument explicitly identifies workers' rights as an additional and ultimately decisive objection to the arrangement.

items.label: C
items.text: Rehabilitation is recognised as a legitimate purpose of prison work, but the argument does not require employers to receive no benefit. Its objection concerns unfair treatment and compensation.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage does not establish that prisoners are replacing regular employees. Its concern is that prisoners may be treated less favourably for performing work.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage raises safety concerns but does not establish that prisoners necessarily lack relevant skills or that only particular professional groups should maintain public services.

main_body.text:
A car journey begins with a 15km drive at an average speed of 60km/hour, then 5hours on the motorway, including two 15-minute rest stops, travelling at an average driving speed of
80km/hour, and finally a 20km drive at an average speed of 40km/hour from the motorway to the destination.

question.main_question: If the destination is reached at 12:00midday, at what time did the journey begin?

blocks.text:
The journey consists of three sections. The first 15km at 60km/h takes 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25 hours, or 15 minutes. The motorway section takes 5 hours in total, including the two 15-minute rest stops. The final 20km at 40km/h takes 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5 hours, or 30 minutes.

Total journey time = 15 minutes + 5 hours + 30 minutes = 5 hours 45 minutes. Subtracting this duration from the arrival time of 12:00 midday gives a departure time of 06:15. Therefore, D is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: 05:18 would give a journey lasting 6 hours 42 minutes, exceeding the stated total by 57 minutes.

items.label: B
items.text: 05:25 would give 6 hours 35 minutes of travel, which is 50 minutes longer than the calculated duration.

items.label: C
items.text: 05:45 would imply a 6-hour-15-minute journey, adding 30 minutes to the stated duration. The two rest stops are already included in the motorway's 5 hours.

items.label: E
items.text: 06:45 would provide only 5 hours 15 minutes before arrival, which is 30 minutes shorter than the required journey.

blocks.text: Shelves must be single pieces at least 40 cm deep, so 30 cm boards cannot be used. A 4 m board at 45 cm depth costs $9.30 and gives two 1.8 m shelves; a 2 m board costs $4.95 and gives one. Buy two 4 m boards and one 2 m board: 2×$9.30+$4.95 = $23.55 for five shelves. This is C.

items.label: E
items.text: $25.50 buys the analogous 60 cm-deep boards, which are more expensive than the sufficient 45 cm depth.

1 Like other booming cities, including New York, London has thrived amid globalisation. It is
growing by 100000 new residents a year. However, if London has given striving people plenty
of reasons to come, it has done a poor job of housing them. The median price of a London
home has tripled over the past two decades. Since 2001 the disposable income of people
renting property has fallen by 30 per cent as a result. Businesses are worried too. Commercial
property in central London is twice as expensive as in New York. Productivity has begun to
slow as promising firms are forced out. Overpriced property is costing London the economic
and human diversity on which its prosperity depends.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?
A London needs striving people in order to prosper.
B Londoners in rented homes have 30 per cent less to spend.
C London has done a poor job of housing its new residents.
D Businesses are worried by the recent slowdown in productivity.
E Expensive property is costing London the diversity it needs to prosper.

question.question_text:
Like other booming cities, including New York, London has thrived amid globalisation. It is growing by 100000 new residents a year. However, if London has given striving people plenty of reasons to come, it has done a poor job of housing them. The median price of a London home has tripled over the past two decades. Since 2001 the disposable income of people renting property has fallen by 30 per cent as a result. Businesses are worried too. Commercial property in central London is twice as expensive as in New York. Productivity has begun to slow as promising firms are forced out. Overpriced property is costing London the economic and human diversity on which its prosperity depends.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
London's prosperity depends on attracting a diverse population of residents and businesses, but rapidly increasing property prices are undermining this advantage. Rising housing costs have reduced renters' disposable income, while expensive commercial property is forcing promising businesses out and slowing productivity.

These consequences support the author's overall conclusion that overpriced property is depriving London of the economic and human diversity essential to its prosperity. Therefore, E expresses the main conclusion.

items.label: A
items.text: The importance of attracting ambitious people helps explain why diversity matters to London's prosperity. However, it is a supporting premise rather than the conclusion about property prices threatening that prosperity.

items.label: B
items.text: The 30% decline in renters' disposable income is evidence of the consequences of rising housing costs, not the author's overall conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: London's failure to provide adequate housing introduces the problem, but the argument extends beyond housing to its consequences for businesses, diversity and economic prosperity.

items.label: D
items.text: Slowing productivity and business concerns illustrate the economic consequences of expensive property. They support the broader conclusion rather than expressing it.

possessed by athletes as they start their training.

main_body.text:
A high degree of self-discipline is one quality exhibited by all athletes who have reached the uppermost levels of competition, whatever the sport. This amount of self-discipline is in evidence long after the initial excitement of a sport has worn off, and an athlete has had to keep going through years of painful and repetitive training sessions. The example of top athletes suggests one approach to improving student behaviour and educational achievement.
If more young people could begin training programmes akin to those of elite athletes, they too would develop exceptional levels of personal discipline to apply within their studies.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument observes that elite athletes demonstrate exceptional self-discipline after years of demanding training. It then assumes that their training developed this discipline and concludes that similar programmes would produce comparable discipline in students.

However, the observed relationship does not establish causation. Athletes may already possess unusually strong self-discipline before beginning training, enabling them to persist through difficult programmes and reach elite levels. If so, training might not produce the same discipline in students who lack this initial characteristic. Therefore, E identifies the flaw: confusing a pre-existing characteristic with an effect of training.

items.label: A
items.text: Elite performance may require abilities beyond self-discipline, but the argument concerns whether training develops discipline, not whether discipline alone guarantees sporting success.

items.label: B
items.text: Other activities might also develop self-discipline, but this does not undermine the possibility that athletic training could develop it.

items.label: C
items.text: Limited access to elite coaching could make similar programmes difficult to implement. However, this is a practical obstacle rather than the underlying causal error about how athletes acquire discipline.

items.label: D
items.text: Educational achievement may not be necessary for success in later life, but this does not address whether athletic training would improve students' discipline or academic performance.

B Some social problems are increasingly problems of middle-aged people.
C People who drink are more likely to engage in criminal activity.
D Drink, drugs and suicide are the biggest killers of middle-aged people.
E Young people are likely to develop harmful behaviours later in life.

main_body.text:
Young people are becoming ever more responsible. They are less likely to take drugs or drink than past generations. Very few have serious problems with alcohol or drugs. It is people in their forties who are most likely to be admitted to hospital for drinking-related problems. The latest figures on drug addiction show that 39% of heroin addicts are now over the age of forty, up from 19% in 2006. Fewer than ever are under the age of twenty-four. The number of young adults in prison is falling, but our overcrowded prisons are increasingly home to the older generation: between 2002 and 2013, the number of middle-aged men locked up increased by
130%. The same is true of suicide rates: on both sides of the Atlantic fewer young people but more middle-aged men are killing themselves.

question.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

blocks.text:
The passage presents evidence that certain harmful behaviours and social problems are becoming less prevalent among younger people while affecting substantial numbers of middle-aged adults. It cites drinking-related hospital admissions, the increasing proportion of heroin addicts over forty, rising imprisonment among middle-aged men and comparatively worsening suicide patterns in that age group.

Together, these examples support the conclusion that some problems traditionally associated with younger people are increasingly affecting middle-aged individuals. Therefore, B is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage compares specific problems involving substance use, imprisonment and suicide. It does not establish that younger people experience fewer health problems overall.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage discusses alcohol-related harm and imprisonment separately but provides no evidence that drinking increases an individual's likelihood of criminal behaviour.

items.label: D
items.text: Although alcohol, drugs and suicide are significant concerns, the passage provides no comparison with other causes of death to establish that they are the biggest killers of middle-aged people.

items.label: E
items.text: The statistics compare age groups at particular times. They do not demonstrate that today's responsible young people will develop harmful behaviours when they become older.

5 Adults thinking back on their experience of school almost always remember with most gratitude
the teachers who taught them more than just a subject, and prepared them for life, not just for
an exam. But the current generation of students may not have the same experiences to look
back on in future years because the role of teachers has changed. The focus for both students
and teachers is now mainly on exam results, and that is how their success or failure is
measured. For teachers to share their lives with their students, offering them a model of
adulthood to which to aspire, is therefore no longer considered desirable. So children today
receive a less valuable education than their parents and grandparents did.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?
A Education for life is of greater value than merely passing exams.
B Adults looking back on their childhood often remember only the good parts.
C Many young people have higher ambitions than becoming like their teachers.
D Exam results are the vital keys which open the door to education and a livelihood.
E Offering students a model of adulthood is a more satisfying role than helping them to pass
exams.
