Adults thinking back on their experience of school almost always remember with most gratitude
the teachers who taught them more than just a subject, and prepared them for life, not just for
an exam. But the current generation of students may not have the same experiences to look
back on in future years because the role of teachers has changed. The focus for both students
and teachers is now mainly on exam results, and that is how their success or failure is
measured. For teachers to share their lives with their students, offering them a model of
adulthood to which to aspire, is therefore no longer considered desirable. So children today
receive a less valuable education than their parents and grandparents did.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Education for life is of greater value than merely passing exams.

options.label: B
options.text: Adults looking back on their childhood often remember only the good parts.

options.label: C
options.text: Many young people have higher ambitions than becoming like their teachers.

options.label: D
options.text: Exam results are the vital keys which open the door to education and a livelihood.

options.label: E
options.text:
Offering students a model of adulthood is a more satisfying role than helping them to pass
exams.

main_body.text: Adults thinking back on their experience of school almost always remember with most gratitude the teachers who taught them more than just a subject, and prepared them for life, not just for an exam. But the current generation of students may not have the same experiences to look back on in future years because the role of teachers has changed. The focus for both students and teachers is now mainly on exam results, and that is how their success or failure is measured. For teachers to share their lives with their students, offering them a model of adulthood to which to aspire, is therefore no longer considered desirable. So children today receive a less valuable education than their parents and grandparents did.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument claims that education today is less valuable because teachers increasingly focus on examination results rather than preparing students for life and providing examples of adulthood.

For this change to constitute a reduction in educational value, preparation for life must be considered more valuable than merely achieving examination success. If examination results were equally or more important, the shift towards exam-focused teaching would not necessarily make education worse. Therefore, A is the underlying assumption connecting the change in teaching priorities to the conclusion about reduced educational value.

items.label: B
items.text: Adults may selectively remember positive school experiences, but the argument does not require this tendency. Such bias could instead weaken the comparison with earlier generations.

items.label: C
items.text: Students may have ambitions different from those of their teachers, but the argument concerns the value of learning from adult role models, not necessarily copying their careers or ambitions.

items.label: D
items.text: Examination results may be important for future opportunities, but this does not establish that exam-focused education is more valuable than broader preparation for life.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument concerns the educational benefits received by students, not whether teachers find mentoring more personally satisfying than helping students pass examinations.

9 Texting is the preferred method of communication among young people, with 72% of teenagers
saying they text regularly and one in three sending more than a hundred texts per day.
Unfortunately, however, very few youngsters seem able to communicate using grammatically
correct sentences. They seem to think it ‘gr8’ that correct spelling is no longer considered
necessary. Many local employers have complained that school-leavers have no idea how to
communicate appropriately, whether face-to-face or in business letters. Many written job
applications are phrased so poorly that they go straight in the bin. Mobile phones were banned
in my daughter’s school last year, a move which has proved fully justified. Since then test
scores in English have improved. All schools need to introduce a similar ban.
Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?
A It makes a false statistical comparison between the 72% of teenagers who merely text
regularly and those who send more than a hundred texts in a day.
B It assumes that, because test scores improved after the ban on mobile phones, the
improvement was due to the ban.
C The argument rests on the assumption that communicating by text is inappropriate.
D Its conclusion, that communicating by text is inappropriate, merely restates one of the
reasons given in support of the argument.
E It assumes that correct spelling is a necessary requirement for gaining employment.

main_body.text:
Texting is the preferred method of communication among young people, with 72% of teenagers saying they text regularly and one in three sending more than a hundred texts per day.
Unfortunately, however, very few youngsters seem able to communicate using grammatically correct sentences. They seem to think it ‘gr8’ that correct spelling is no longer considered necessary. Many local employers have complained that school-leavers have no idea how to communicate appropriately, whether face-to-face or in business letters. Many written job applications are phrased so poorly that they go straight in the bin. Mobile phones were banned in my daughter’s school last year, a move which has proved fully justified. Since then test scores in English have improved. All schools need to introduce a similar ban.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument states that mobile phones were banned in the author's daughter's school and that English test scores subsequently improved. It treats this sequence as evidence that the ban caused the improvement and uses it to recommend equivalent bans in every school.

However, an improvement occurring after a policy change does not establish that the policy caused it. Other changes in teaching, assessment or student performance could explain the higher scores. Without identifying the cause, the argument cannot reliably attribute the improvement to the phone ban. Therefore, B identifies the flaw.

items.label: A
items.text: The two texting statistics describe different frequencies of texting, but the argument does not make the statistical comparison alleged. Its decisive inference concerns the cause of improved examination scores.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage criticises poor spelling and inappropriate communication, not necessarily every use of text messaging. The proposed ban depends on the claimed educational benefits rather than treating all texting as inherently inappropriate.

items.label: D
items.text: The main conclusion recommends banning mobile phones in schools, not that texting itself is inappropriate. The argument therefore does not merely restate a premise as its conclusion.

items.label: E
items.text: Poor spelling may harm job applications, but the passage does not establish that perfect spelling is required for every job. This stronger assumption is unnecessary to the argument about school phone bans.

who revealed their gender on the website and those who did not.
D Even by modern standards, Ada Lovelace received an extensive education in mathematics
and the sciences.
E Male contributors to the website experienced a similar drop in their code change
acceptance rates when their gender was revealed.

main_body.text: While it is a woman, Ada Lovelace, who is often credited with originating the concept of software, today’s computer tech-related jobs are held mostly by men. The tech sector must continue to work against factors that inhibit gender equality within it. One such factor appears to be prejudice about women’s abilities to write computer programming code. A recent study of a program-sharing and development website analysed the rates by which suggested code changes were accepted by website users according to the gender of the user contributing the changes. In cases where the contributor’s gender was not made clear on the website, 72 per cent of the suggestions made by women were accepted. In cases where the contributor’s gender was revealed to be female, the acceptance rate fell to 63 per cent.

question.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument suggests prejudice against female programmers because code changes submitted by women were accepted 72% of the time when their gender was hidden, compared with 63% when it was revealed.

However, E states that male contributors experienced a similar decline when their gender became visible. This introduces an alternative explanation: revealing a contributor's gender, or the associated visibility of their identity, may affect acceptance rates generally rather than reflecting prejudice specifically against women. Therefore, E most weakens the inference that the observed decline demonstrates gender-specific discrimination against female programmers.

items.label: A
items.text: Female users rejecting more code changes concerns their behaviour as reviewers, not whether other users discriminate against female contributors whose gender is visible.

items.label: B
items.text: Initiatives encouraging women to enter programming show efforts to improve representation, but they do not establish whether bias affected the acceptance rates in the study.

items.label: C
items.text: If the two groups of female contributors submitted code of similar quality, differences in the code itself would become a less plausible explanation for the acceptance-rate gap. This would strengthen the discrimination hypothesis.

items.label: D
items.text: Ada Lovelace's scientific education provides historical background but does not explain the difference between acceptance rates for identified and unidentified female contributors.

blocks.text:
The first lamp alternates between 1 second on and 1 second off, repeating every 2 seconds. The second alternates between 2 seconds on and 2 seconds off, repeating every 4 seconds. Both are switched on simultaneously.

Over each 4-second cycle, the first lamp is off during seconds 1–2 and 3–4, while the second is off during seconds 2–4. Therefore, both lamps are off together only during seconds 3–4, for exactly 1 second per 4-second cycle.

There are 60 ÷ 4 = 15 complete cycles in one minute, giving 15 × 1 = 15 seconds of simultaneous darkness. Therefore, C is correct.

items.label: D

items.label: E
items.text: 30 seconds is the total time each individual lamp spends switched off during a minute. It does not account for the other lamp remaining illuminated during some of those intervals.

main_body.text:
Recently a pioneering natural flood management scheme slowed river peak flow by 15 to
20 per cent, saving a small town’s museum and several homes. As part of this scheme, special dams, designed to leak water gradually, were installed in nearby hills to slow the flow of water off the slopes. An upstream flood storage reservoir was installed, along with the planting of thousands of trees and the restoration of heather moorland, which acted as a sponge. Around half of the reduction in flood water in the town was due to the upstream land management measures, and half due to the effect of the flood storage area. Natural flood management measures improve water quality, prevent erosion and, in some cases, store carbon.

question.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

blocks.text:
The passage describes a natural flood management scheme that successfully reduced peak river flow and protected buildings. It then identifies additional environmental benefits of the methods used: improving water quality, preventing erosion and, in some cases, storing carbon.

These effects are separate from the immediate reduction of flooding. Therefore, the evidence establishes that natural flood management can provide benefits beyond flood prevention. This is the conclusion expressed in B.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage reports that the scheme reduced flood risk in one case but provides no evidence about its effectiveness under exceptionally heavy rainfall.

items.label: C
items.text: The reduction in floodwater was attributed approximately equally to upstream land management and flood storage, but this does not establish that every natural flood management method is equally effective.

items.label: D
items.text: The success of one scheme does not establish that natural flood management is suitable or necessary in every flood-prone location.

items.label: E
items.text: The described scheme involved hills and upstream land management, but the passage provides no comparison with schemes in other landscapes to establish where these methods are most effective.

main_body.text: The government is planning an increase in fuel tax later this year as part of its strategy to meet carbon emissions targets. Yet motorists and road transport companies have suffered crippling price rises of up to 30% in petrol and diesel bills in the past year because of fuel taxes. The government has enjoyed a £505 million windfall from high oil prices in the last six months alone, with extra revenue coming from North Sea oil reserves. A further increase in fuel tax will impact on all UK households because it will eventually push up the price of shop goods and inflation. So the government must abandon its planned tax increase.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above passage?

blocks.text:
The government plans to increase fuel tax to help meet carbon emissions targets. The argument opposes this policy because fuel costs have already increased substantially and higher taxes would raise transport costs, consumer prices and inflation.

For these economic consequences to justify abandoning a policy intended to reduce emissions, the argument must assume that protecting people's finances takes priority over the environmental objective in this situation. If controlling emissions were considered more important, the government could reasonably accept the financial costs. Therefore, A is the underlying assumption.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument calls for abandoning a proposed increase, not necessarily reducing existing fuel prices. It does not require fuel costs to fall below their current level.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument acknowledges emissions reduction as the government's objective but does not need to assume that no other justification for higher fuel taxes could exist.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage describes financial pressure on transport companies, but the proposed recommendation does not depend on those companies actually facing bankruptcy.

items.label: E
items.text: Additional oil revenue is mentioned as evidence of the government's financial position. The argument does not require this revenue to be used specifically to reduce existing fuel taxes.

Husbands and wives have a lower risk of disease and a higher life expectancy. They smoke less, drink less and eat more healthily. Those who get married and stay married have on average double the amount of wealth of those who never marry. Surveys show that they are happier than single people and less likely to experience mid-life depression. Married couples benefit from stronger networks of support, with relatives providing more care and assistance in old age and in times of need. question.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above reasoning?

blocks.text:
The argument uses the observation that married people tend to be wealthier, healthier and happier to recommend pursuing marriage. This reasoning assumes that marriage itself contributes to these advantages rather than merely being associated with them.

E weakens this inference by stating that wealthier couples are four times more likely to marry than poorer couples. This suggests an alternative explanation for married people's greater average wealth: people who are already financially better off may be more likely to get married. Therefore, the observed association between marriage and wealth does not necessarily show that marriage produces greater wealth. This weakens an important part of the argument supporting marriage.

items.label: A
items.text: Evidence that marriage improves cancer survival would support the claim that marriage contributes to better health outcomes.

items.label: B
items.text: Differences in whether married people have children might complicate the statistics, but the option does not establish that parenthood explains the reported advantages.

items.label: C
items.text: Tax advantages for married couples could help explain why marriage contributes to greater wealth. This supports rather than undermines the claimed financial benefits.

items.label: D
items.text: Conflict-ridden relationships may be associated with poorer health, showing that relationship quality matters. However, this does not directly challenge the claim about married people's average advantages as strongly as the selection effect identified in E.

main_body.text:
Three friends are training to run a marathon. Part of this training involves running steadily round a track in the local park. They are all at different stages in their training schedules so they run at different speeds. Alec completes each lap in 3 minutes, Barry takes 5 minutes and Colin takes 6 minutes.
They all leave the start line at the same time.

question.main_question: If they each maintain their running speed throughout the session, how many more laps will Alec have completed compared to Barry when the three of them next cross the start line together?

blocks.text:
The three runners complete one lap every 3, 5 and 6 minutes respectively. For all three to cross the start line simultaneously again, the elapsed time must be a common multiple of all three lap times.

The lowest common multiple of 3, 5 and 6 is 30 minutes. In that time, Alec completes 30 ÷ 3 = 10 laps, while Barry completes 30 ÷ 5 = 6 laps.

The difference is 10 − 6 = 4 laps. Therefore, B is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: 2 laps is below the calculated difference of 4 at the first time all three runners return to the start line together.

items.label: C
items.text: 5 laps exceeds the difference between Alec's 10 completed laps and Barry's 6 completed laps by one.

items.label: D
items.text: 6 is the number of laps Barry completes in 30 minutes, not the number of additional laps completed by Alec.

items.label: E
items.text: 10 is Alec's total number of completed laps at the next simultaneous crossing, not his lead over Barry.

conservation of the Arctic ecosystem.

some species of animal.

main_body.text:
It is universally recognised that Africa’s conservation tourism provides employment, generates wealth and educates future generations while saving endangered species. So we should champion tourism for the sake of conservation. Tourism in the Arctic is thus to be welcomed.
As the Arctic ice melts, new shipping routes are opening up. It is unfair to characterise the presence of a large cruise ship in the Northwest Passage as ‘extinction tourism’ that merely indulges people who want to view endangered animals before it is too late. The tourists will return home better informed about the Arctic’s fragile ecosystem.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

blocks.text: The argument uses the success of conservation tourism in Africa to justify welcoming tourism in the Arctic. However, evidence that tourism generates wealth, employment and conservation benefits in one region does not establish that it will produce comparable benefits elsewhere. The Arctic may face different conditions, and the passage provides no evidence that cruise tourism there will protect endangered species or support conservation as African tourism allegedly does. Therefore, A identifies the flaw: generalising from one successful example of wildlife tourism to tourism in other environments.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument explicitly challenges the claim that tourists merely want to see endangered animals, suggesting that they may also gain knowledge. It does not assume that viewing animals is their only motivation.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument presents tourism as beneficial because it supports conservation. It does not treat tourism as more important than successful conservation.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage predicts that tourists will return better informed, but it does not require them to become committed conservationists. Its broader weakness is extending the African example to the Arctic.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument presents conservation tourism as helping endangered species survive, not as inevitably causing their extinction.

main_body.text:
If the vice president did act unlawfully in this matter, he would definitely have had to resign.
Since we have confirmation that he has resigned, he must have broken the law.

question.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The original argument states that unlawful conduct would require the vice president to resign. It then observes that he has resigned and concludes that he must have acted unlawfully. This incorrectly treats a consequence as proof of its proposed cause: resignation could occur for reasons other than unlawful conduct.

E follows the same pattern. It states that a venomous snake bite would cause severe inflammation, then concludes that the snake must have been venomous because inflammation is present. Both arguments affirm the consequent: if P then Q; Q occurs; therefore P. This inference is invalid because Q may have other causes.

items.label: A
items.text: This applies the contrapositive: if a king cobra bite guarantees death, survival rules out a king cobra bite. It does not infer a cause from the presence of its consequence.

items.label: B
items.text: Yellow markings are presented as sufficient evidence of a pit viper, and the conclusion applies that condition directly. This is not the same reversed inference.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument rules out the stated rattlesnake danger because rattlesnakes are absent, rather than inferring the original cause from an observed consequence.

items.label: D
items.text: This reasons from receiving prompt treatment to the absence of complications, although the original conditional only concerns delayed treatment. It denies the antecedent rather than affirming the consequent.

housing people with mental health problems in remote areas with no contact with the general
population. So we have to accept that these projects can only work if we live near, and interact
with, the people they are designed to help. Practise what you preach!

many electronic gadgets.
D People who choose to be vegetarians should seek to persuade others not to eat meat or
fish.
E People who have benefitted from grants or bursaries for university education should lobby
for others to have the same advantages.

main_body.text: It’s common for people to agree in principle to socially useful projects such as the opening of centres for people with serious mental health problems. However, if the project is planned for the area where they live, they tend to object and suggest that alternative locations would be preferable. While they approve of the general idea of such projects, they won’t tolerate any negative effects on their own lives. We really don’t want to go back to outdated practices of housing people with mental health problems in remote areas with no contact with the general population. blocks.text:
The argument establishes that people who support socially beneficial projects must be willing to accept the personal inconvenience or cost necessary for those projects to succeed. Supporting a mental health centre in principle while refusing to live near its users is inconsistent because integration into ordinary communities is essential to the proposed approach.

B illustrates the same principle. People who support increased healthcare funding should accept the higher taxes required to finance it rather than supporting the benefit while objecting to their personal contribution. Both arguments require consistency between endorsing a collective benefit and accepting its individual costs.

items.label: A
items.text: Refusing to support sporting events because of corruption concerns expresses consistency between criticism and consumer behaviour, but it does not specifically concern accepting a personal cost necessary to provide a public benefit.

items.label: C
items.text: Parents limiting their children's access to gadgets would make their actions consistent with their beliefs, but the issue concerns private parenting choices rather than sharing the burdens of a socially beneficial project.

items.label: D
items.text: Vegetarians encouraging others to adopt their diet extends a personal conviction to other people. It does not require them to accept personal disadvantages associated with a collective policy they support.

items.label: E
items.text: Supporting access to benefits previously received by oneself concerns extending opportunities to others, not accepting the personal costs of implementing a publicly supported project.

blocks.text: Count how often each fixed segment is used by digits 1–9; do not count the total segments in a single digit. The lower-right segment appears in every digit except 2, so its count is 8. The lower-left appears only in 2, 6 and 8, giving 3. The other segment counts lie between these limits. Thus the maximum/minimum pair is 8 and 3, C.

items.label: A
items.text: The maximum exceeds 7 because the lower-right segment lights for eight digits; the minimum is 3 rather than 4.

items.label: B
items.text: Both limits are wrong: the lower-right reaches 8 and the lower-left is used only 3 times, not 5.

items.label: D
items.text: Its maximum of 8 is correct, but the minimum of 5 overlooks the sparsely used lower-left segment.

items.label: E
items.text: No segment appears in all nine digits; even the lower-right is off for 2, and the minimum is below 4.

blocks.text: The route has three straight runs, each of two rolls: right, down, right. Two rolls in one direction swap the top and bottom faces. Three such swaps therefore leave the face opposite the initial top facing up. Folding the pictured net puts the rectangle opposite the triangle. Since the triangle starts on top, the rectangle finishes on top: D.

items.label: A
items.text: The square is adjacent to the triangle in the net, not opposite it; it cannot be the result of the three top/bottom swaps.

items.label: C
items.text: The triangle would return to the top after an even number of these two-roll runs; there are three runs.

items.label: E
items.text: The ring is another adjacent face, so it does not occupy the final opposite-top position.

27 People are quick to connect attempts to reduce the effects of climate change with the
protection of the environment. However, responding to climate change is much more important
for humanity than for nature. In the history of the planet, the relative stability of temperatures in
the last ten thousand years is the exception rather than the norm. Nature has always found a
way to adapt to large temperature variations but human civilisations, all of which have evolved

E Nature will find a way to adapt, but climate change is potentially devastating for humans.

main_body.text: People are quick to connect attempts to reduce the effects of climate change with the protection of the environment. However, responding to climate change is much more important for humanity than for nature. In the history of the planet, the relative stability of temperatures in the last ten thousand years is the exception rather than the norm. Nature has always found a way to adapt to large temperature variations but human civilisations, all of which have evolved in the last ten thousand years, have developed in a period with unusually reliable and predictable weather. question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument contrasts nature's historical ability to adapt to major temperature changes with humanity's dependence on comparatively stable climatic conditions. Human civilisations developed during an unusually predictable period, whereas the natural world has experienced much greater fluctuations throughout Earth's history.

The author uses this difference to argue that climate change poses a more serious threat to human civilisation than to nature's long-term survival. Therefore, B expresses the main conclusion: action against climate change is more important for humanity than for the environment.

items.label: A
items.text: The association between climate policy and environmental protection introduces the argument. The author challenges this emphasis rather than presenting it as the main conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: Nature's historical adaptation to temperature changes is supporting evidence explaining why climate change may threaten humans more severely.

items.label: D
items.text: The development of civilisation during a relatively stable climatic period helps explain human vulnerability. It is a premise supporting the comparative conclusion.

items.label: E
items.text: This summarises the contrasting consequences for nature and humans, but it primarily explains why responding to climate change is more important for humanity. B expresses that broader conclusion about the priority of action.

28 Chiropractors rely heavily on manipulating their patients’ spines. This has benefits for some
patients, but more than half of all patients suffer mild to moderate adverse effects after seeing a
chiropractor. These are mostly local and referred pains that usually last for two to three days.
Chiropractors often claim that these are necessary steps on the road to getting better.
However, several hundred cases have been documented in which patients were seriously and
often permanently damaged after chiropractic manipulations. What usually happens in these
tragic instances is that, upon manipulation of the upper spine, an artery supplying the brain is
overstretched and simply breaks up, leading to a stroke that can prove fatal.
Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?
A Chiropractic therapy should be banned.
B Chiropractic therapy may do more harm than good.
C The spine is the most delicate part of the human body.
D People should see a doctor before going to a chiropractor.
E Pain is a necessary part of the healing process.

Chiropractors rely heavily on manipulating their patients’ spines. This has benefits for some patients, but more than half of all patients suffer mild to moderate adverse effects after seeing a chiropractor. These are mostly local and referred pains that usually last for two to three days.
Chiropractors often claim that these are necessary steps on the road to getting better.
However, several hundred cases have been documented in which patients were seriously and often permanently damaged after chiropractic manipulations. What usually happens in these tragic instances is that, upon manipulation of the upper spine, an artery supplying the brain is overstretched and simply breaks up, leading to a stroke that can prove fatal.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?

blocks.text:
The passage acknowledges that chiropractic spinal manipulation benefits some patients, but reports that more than half experience mild or moderate adverse effects. It also describes several hundred cases involving serious, sometimes permanent injuries, including strokes following damage to arteries supplying the brain.

These risks establish that chiropractic treatment can produce harm, sometimes severe, despite its possible benefits. The evidence therefore supports the cautious conclusion that chiropractic therapy may do more harm than good, as stated in B. It does not establish that harm necessarily outweighs benefits in every case.

items.label: A
items.text: The reported risks raise safety concerns, but the passage also acknowledges benefits for some patients. It does not establish that banning all chiropractic treatment is necessary.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage identifies particular risks associated with spinal manipulation but makes no comparison between the spine and other parts of the body.

items.label: D
items.text: Consulting a doctor beforehand might be a precaution, but the passage provides no evidence that doing so would prevent the described injuries.

items.label: E
items.text: The claim that adverse effects are necessary for recovery is attributed to chiropractors. The passage does not establish that pain is an essential part of healing.

It is no surprise that the number of motorists opting for re-education courses has tripled in five years, but the high cost of such courses has led to accusations that police forces might use the new system for their own benefit. They could easily set up speed traps, catch a number of motorists slightly over the limit, and generate easy income for themselves. Re-education courses are a good idea in theory, but open to abuse by cash-starved police forces.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument warns that police forces might exploit re-education courses to generate income by catching motorists committing relatively minor offences and collecting course fees. For this proposed financial incentive to exist, the money collected from participants must exceed the cost of providing the courses.

If the courses cost as much as or more than the fees collected, increasing participation would not generate the surplus revenue described. Therefore, A is the underlying assumption necessary for the argument that police forces could benefit financially from expanding the scheme.

items.label: B
items.text: The concern is that police might exploit courses for revenue, not that re-education prevents offences more effectively than conventional penalties.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument suggests that financial pressure could create incentives for abuse. It does not require police forces to be generally more interested in income than road safety.

items.label: D
items.text: The number of people choosing courses has tripled, but this does not establish that the total number of driving offences has tripled. The financial concern does not require such an increase.

items.label: E
items.text: Drivers' preferences between penalty points and financial costs might affect their choices, but the argument about police revenue does not depend on one fear being greater than the other.

raw.question_block:
33 A band of rebellious traders in Wales has decided to take their whole town ‘offshore’ in protest
at the insignificant amounts of UK tax paid by big businesses. An alliance of shopkeepers from
the town want to use the same controversial loopholes favoured by huge multinationals such
as Google so that they too can legally avoid UK tax. The coffee giant Starbucks, for
example, has been branded immoral for transferring revenues out of the UK and into the
Netherlands and Switzerland, where they receive sweetened tax deals. But the shopkeepers of
the town cannot have it both ways. If they believe it is immoral for Starbucks to avoid UK tax, it
is immoral for them, too. They should continue to pay UK tax in full.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?
A The sole purpose of the protest is to pressure the government into tackling tax avoidance
by big business.
B If the shopkeepers are successful, every town could follow their lead, harming the UK
economy even further.
C Small businesses acting alone cannot obtain the same tax breaks as the giant
corporations.
D Every time the government comes up with a way of tackling tax avoidance, lawyers simply
find a new loophole.
E One of the town traders found that last year he paid seven times more corporation tax than
Facebook.

An alliance of shopkeepers from the town want to use the same controversial loopholes favoured by huge multinationals such as Google so that they too can legally avoid UK tax. question.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument claims that Welsh shopkeepers would be acting inconsistently if they avoided UK taxes while condemning large corporations for doing the same. It therefore concludes that the shopkeepers should continue paying their taxes in full.

A weakens this criticism by explaining that the shopkeepers' sole purpose is to pressure the government into tackling corporate tax avoidance. Their proposed actions would then be a form of protest against the system rather than an attempt to gain the same financial advantages they condemn. This difference in purpose provides a reason to distinguish the morality of their protest from the corporations' tax-avoidance practices.

items.label: B
items.text: If similar protests harmed the economy, this would provide an additional reason to oppose the shopkeepers' actions rather than weaken the argument against them.

items.label: C
items.text: Small businesses being unable to obtain the same tax benefits would question the feasibility of the proposed scheme, but it would not undermine the principle that comparable tax avoidance should be judged consistently.

items.label: D
items.text: The existence of continually emerging loopholes explains difficulties in addressing tax avoidance but does not establish that shopkeepers are morally justified in using those loopholes.

items.label: E
items.text: The difference between one trader's taxes and Facebook's taxes may explain the protest, but unequal payments alone do not establish that avoiding taxes is morally acceptable for the trader.

raw.question_block:
34 Much concern is paid to the hazards posed by people using mobile phones while operating
motor vehicles. Although using a smartphone or other mobile phone behind the wheel of a car
is most certainly dangerous, research is showing that very frequent usage of the phones is
harmful more generally. A study has found that individuals with relatively high levels of mobile
phone usage are more likely to demonstrate cognitive failures, which can range from forgetting
appointments to accidentally bumping into things in the environment. Cognitive failures are
associated with the short attention spans also observed in high-frequency mobile phone users.
Clearly, if people want to reduce their risk of cognitive failures, they should limit the amount of
time they spend on their mobile phones.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?
A High-frequency mobile phone users may have had short attention spans prior to the
formation of their phone usage habits.
B Limiting one’s smartphone or mobile phone usage may not be a sufficient strategy for
significantly reducing cognitive failures.
C Mobile phones may play an important role in the completion of everyday tasks in the lives
of many people.
D Smartphones and other mobile phones may have different applications or features that are
not all used in the exact same fashion.
E The risks posed by using a mobile phone while driving may be much greater than those
posed by too-frequent usage of the phones overall.

main_body.text:
Much concern is paid to the hazards posed by people using mobile phones while operating motor vehicles. Although using a smartphone or other mobile phone behind the wheel of a car is most certainly dangerous, research is showing that very frequent usage of the phones is harmful more generally. A study has found that individuals with relatively high levels of mobile phone usage are more likely to demonstrate cognitive failures, which can range from forgetting appointments to accidentally bumping into things in the environment. Cognitive failures are associated with the short attention spans also observed in high-frequency mobile phone users.
Clearly, if people want to reduce their risk of cognitive failures, they should limit the amount of time they spend on their mobile phones.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument observes that frequent mobile phone users are more likely to experience cognitive failures and short attention spans. It then concludes that reducing phone use will lower the risk of these problems.

However, this assumes that frequent phone use causes the observed cognitive difficulties. A identifies an alternative explanation: individuals might already have short attention spans before developing their phone habits. Such people could be more inclined to use phones frequently, meaning their pre-existing characteristics help explain the association. If so, reducing phone use might not resolve the underlying cause. Therefore, A identifies the causal flaw.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument recommends limiting phone use to reduce risk, not eliminating every cognitive failure. A strategy need not be sufficient on its own to produce some reduction in risk.

items.label: C
items.text: Phones may provide practical benefits in everyday life, but those benefits do not establish whether frequent usage causes cognitive problems.

items.label: D
items.text: Different phone functions may involve different activities, but the option does not identify an alternative cause of the observed association between frequent use and cognitive failures.

items.label: E
items.text: The relative danger of phone use while driving concerns a different risk. It does not determine whether general phone use causes the cognitive difficulties described.

D It is possible to think of hypocrisy as a good thing.
E Hypocrisy is a serious moral weakness.

main_body.text: Nearly everyone thinks it is a bad thing to be a hypocrite, because it is profoundly dishonest to pretend to have moral standards that you do not actually have. But pretending you are better than you are is evidence that you still accept the moral principles you have failed to follow. So it is better than being shameless about your moral failings. Perceived in this way, hypocrisy can be considered to be a virtue. Being a hypocrite shows you feel a need to hide some aspect of your life because it would be too embarrassing to allow it into the open. Many hypocrites wish they were the people they pretend to be: so perhaps one day they will succeed.

question.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument challenges the conventional judgement that hypocrisy is necessarily bad. Although hypocrites fail to follow the moral standards they profess, their desire to appear morally better suggests that they still recognise those standards as desirable.

This distinguishes hypocrisy from openly disregarding moral principles. The passage also suggests that some hypocrites genuinely aspire to become the people they pretend to be, potentially leading to improvement. These considerations support the author's central conclusion that hypocrisy can sometimes be regarded as a virtue rather than exclusively as a moral failing. Therefore, D is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: The desire to conceal embarrassing behaviour is presented as evidence that hypocrites recognise moral standards. It supports the conclusion rather than expressing the broader judgement about hypocrisy.

items.label: B
items.text: The criticism of shamelessness helps explain why hypocrisy might be preferable to openly disregarding morality, but it is not the main conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: The possibility of future moral improvement is one reason for evaluating hypocrisy more positively. The conclusion is broader than this potential consequence.

items.label: E
items.text: This reflects the conventional negative view of hypocrisy that the author explicitly challenges by presenting reasons for a more favourable interpretation.

blocks.text: First require 1600×700 mm, side grips and no pre-drilled tap holes. The qualifying steel baths are Europa £126 and Sierra £128; the qualifying acrylic baths are Carola £130 and Victory £149. The cheapest steel and acrylic choices are therefore £126 and £130. The saving is £4, C.

items.text: £10 uses a different price comparison; the only least-cost qualifying pair differs by £4.

items.text: £18 compares Carola £130 with Dalton £112, but Dalton has no side grips and is ineligible.

39 One of the greatest achievements of English grammar schools was the development and
dissemination of a sophisticated system of standard punctuation for the English language. The
complex rules for the use of commas conveyed a range of precise meanings, while the choice
between semi-colon, colon and full stop expressed the exact, and often subtle, relationship
between statements. Without this kind of attention to punctuation, there is bound to be a loss of
precision in communication and in thinking. The current use of commas to join statements
together, without any regard for grammar or the nature of the link between them, lacks rigour
and covers up lazy thinking.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above?
A Most writers do not want to waste time thinking through the exact connections between
their ideas.
B Only a minority of people ever grasped the finer aspects of the traditional system of
punctuation.
C Schools should go back to teaching the traditional system of punctuation.
D The government should reintroduce grammar schools into the UK.
E The vocabulary and grammar of a language naturally evolve over time, and the same is
true of punctuation.

main_body.text: One of the greatest achievements of English grammar schools was the development and dissemination of a sophisticated system of standard punctuation for the English language. The complex rules for the use of commas conveyed a range of precise meanings, while the choice between semi-colon, colon and full stop expressed the exact, and often subtle, relationship between statements. Without this kind of attention to punctuation, there is bound to be a loss of precision in communication and in thinking. The current use of commas to join statements together, without any regard for grammar or the nature of the link between them, lacks rigour and covers up lazy thinking.

question.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above?

blocks.text:
The passage argues that traditional punctuation rules enabled writers to communicate precise relationships between ideas. Commas, semicolons, colons and full stops served different functions, allowing subtle distinctions in meaning.

The author criticises contemporary punctuation practices for disregarding these distinctions, thereby reducing precision in communication and encouraging imprecise thinking. Since traditional punctuation is presented as providing valuable clarity that current practices often lack, the passage supports restoring its instruction in schools. Therefore, C is the conclusion that can be drawn.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage criticises careless punctuation as reflecting lazy thinking, but it does not establish that most writers deliberately avoid considering relationships between their ideas.

items.label: B
items.text: The author praises the traditional system's precision but provides no evidence about how many people successfully mastered its finer rules.

items.label: D
items.text: Grammar schools are praised for their contribution to punctuation standards, but this does not establish that the entire grammar-school system should be reintroduced.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage criticises contemporary changes in punctuation rather than arguing that such changes are necessarily natural or desirable because language evolves.

40 Long hours and poor pay have become commonly accepted, but they are taking a heavy toll on
life at home. It is not a pretty picture: an economy where high levels of stress and anxiety are
normal, where people get ill because they have lost control of their time, and where marriages
are damaged and children suffer. Yet it is a situation that politicians invite us to applaud. They
praise ‘strivers’ and ‘hard-working people’, not chilled-out, caring mums and dads. The longer
and harder we work, the more admirable we are supposed to be. So the political slogans have
clearly been effective, but the resulting glorification of work has made us miserable.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?
A Most employees are not satisfied with their salary.
B Political slogans significantly affect people’s everyday behaviour.
C Restructuring the working week would be beneficial for the economy.
D Companies could afford shorter hours or better pay for their employees.
E People who experience less stress at work are better parents.

main_body.text: Long hours and poor pay have become commonly accepted, but they are taking a heavy toll on life at home. It is not a pretty picture: an economy where high levels of stress and anxiety are normal, where people get ill because they have lost control of their time, and where marriages are damaged and children suffer. Yet it is a situation that politicians invite us to applaud. They praise ‘strivers’ and ‘hard-working people’, not chilled-out, caring mums and dads. The longer and harder we work, the more admirable we are supposed to be. So the political slogans have clearly been effective, but the resulting glorification of work has made us miserable.

question.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument claims that politicians praise relentless work and present longer hours as evidence of admirable character. It then concludes that these political messages have successfully encouraged the glorification of work, contributing to stress, damaged relationships and unhappiness.

For political slogans to be responsible for this outcome, they must meaningfully influence how people behave or what working habits they adopt. If slogans had no significant effect on everyday behaviour, the argument could not attribute the harmful work culture to their success. Therefore, B is the underlying assumption.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage mentions poor pay, but dissatisfaction with salaries is not necessary to establish that political messages encourage excessive working hours.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument criticises the social consequences of overwork but does not require restructuring the working week to benefit economic performance.

items.label: D
items.text: Whether employers could afford shorter hours or higher wages concerns possible solutions, not the assumed influence of political rhetoric on working habits.

items.label: E
items.text: Stress may affect family relationships, but the argument does not require a general comparison establishing that less-stressed workers are better parents.

41 Despite recent improvements to their training, a new study suggests that the police are as
susceptible as the general public to holding false beliefs about crime and punishment.
Participants in the study were questioned about their views on a number of crime-related myths
such as ‘capital punishment is an effective way to deter criminal activity’ – myths, because they
are unsupported by research evidence. Police were just as likely to endorse the
misconceptions as the lay participants and, moreover, were more confident in their false
beliefs. This is a worrying example of a ‘scientist–practitioner gap’, a term which describes a
situation where professionals do not accept the evidence of research relevant to their roles.
Studies have shown that training can permanently reduce the ‘scientist–practitioner gap’. Police
officers need more training.
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?
A The recruitment process for new police officers often fails to identify false beliefs held by
applicants.
B The majority of police officers do not support the return of capital punishment.
C The science–practitioner gap is a common phenomenon in many professions, not just the
police.
D Police training has often been criticised in the media for being insufficiently practical.
E Police officers whose views are not evidence-based are more likely to have complaints
made against them by members of the public.

main_body.text:
Despite recent improvements to their training, a new study suggests that the police are as susceptible as the general public to holding false beliefs about crime and punishment.
Participants in the study were questioned about their views on a number of crime-related myths such as ‘capital punishment is an effective way to deter criminal activity’ – myths, because they are unsupported by research evidence. Police were just as likely to endorse the misconceptions as the lay participants and, moreover, were more confident in their false beliefs. This is a worrying example of a ‘scientist–practitioner gap’, a term which describes a situation where professionals do not accept the evidence of research relevant to their roles.
Studies have shown that training can permanently reduce the ‘scientist–practitioner gap’. Police officers need more training.

question.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

blocks.text:
The argument identifies a gap between research evidence and police officers' beliefs about crime and punishment. Officers are reported to endorse unsupported misconceptions and to express considerable confidence in those beliefs. It then recommends additional training because research indicates that training can reduce this scientist–practitioner gap.

E strengthens the recommendation by establishing that officers whose views are not evidence-based are more likely to receive public complaints. This connects the identified problem with adverse professional consequences, providing an additional practical reason to address misconceptions through training.

items.label: A
items.text: Recruitment failing to identify misconceptions suggests another source of the problem, but it does not directly establish that officers' existing false beliefs have harmful consequences or that additional training is especially important.

items.label: B
items.text: Opposition to capital punishment does not establish that officers avoid other crime-related misconceptions. It offers little support for the recommendation.

items.label: C
items.text: The existence of similar gaps in other professions shows that the problem is widespread, but it does not establish the consequences of such beliefs among police officers.

items.label: D
items.text: Criticism that training is insufficiently practical concerns the character of existing programmes, not specifically whether additional evidence-based training would correct misconceptions.

45 An accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant in Japan in 2011 caused the release of
radioactive material, resulting in around half a million people being evacuated from the area.
These people have not been allowed to return to the area because of the health risks of
exposure to radiation. But the psychological consequences of long-term evacuation may be
more significant than the physical effects of radiation. People who wish to return to live in the
area around Fukushima should be allowed to. Studies of a similar situation at Chernobyl
showed that average life expectancy for evacuees reduced – not predominantly because of
cancer caused by radiation, but because of depression, alcoholism and suicide due to the
impact of permanent evacuation. There is, moreover, massive disagreement in the scientific
community over how much radiation is ‘safe’.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?
A The increased risks of cancer due to exposure to radiation have been exaggerated.
B There is no consensus among scientists about what constitutes a safe level of radiation.
C People who are forcibly evacuated from their homes experience reduced life expectancy.
D People should be allowed to make their own decisions about living in the affected area.
E The negative effects of radiation may be less significant than the psychological
consequences of evacuation.

E follows the same chain. Fixing the car requires good knowledge of it, and arriving at the wedding on time requires fixing the car. items.text: The argument eliminates one of two alternative destinations and infers the other. It does not follow a chain of necessary conditions.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument uses the absence of hearing damage to rule out loud music through earphones. This is a single contrapositive rather than the linked necessary conditions in the original argument.

main_body.text:
Sourdough, an ingredient of many bread products, is a fermented mixture of flour and water. At
8:00am on Monday morning, I start with a mixture of 50g flour and 50g water. Each morning at
8:00am I double the weight of the sourdough by adding equal weights of flour and water.
I know that 1g of the water content evaporates every hour.
The bread recipe that I would like to use requires 500g of sourdough. I also want at least 50g of sourdough left over so that I can continue growing it for next week’s bread.

question.main_question: On which day am I going to have the necessary amount of sourdough?

blocks.text:
The baker needs 500g for the recipe and at least 50g remaining, so the total sourdough required is 550g. The mixture initially weighs 100g on Monday morning. It loses 1g of water per hour, or 24g between daily additions. Each morning, its remaining weight is doubled by adding equal weights of flour and water.

Tuesday: (100 − 24) × 2 = 152g.
Wednesday: (152 − 24) × 2 = 256g.
Thursday: (256 − 24) × 2 = 464g.
Friday: (464 − 24) × 2 = 880g.

Thursday's amount is insufficient, but Friday's exceeds 550g. Therefore, D is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: Tuesday's mixture weighs only 152g after doubling, which is 398g below the required 550g.

items.label: B
items.text: Wednesday's mixture weighs 256g, still 294g below the minimum required for baking and retaining a starter.

items.label: C
items.text: Thursday's mixture weighs 464g, which is 86g short of the required 550g.

items.label: E
items.text: Saturday is later than necessary because the mixture first reaches the required amount on Friday.

main_body.text: A 250g bag of mixed nuts lists the contents on the packet as follows:
As they are my favourite, I eat all the almonds in the packet and then re-weigh it. I find that the almond content was the minimum it could have been whilst being consistent with the labelling.

question.main_question: What is the largest possible peanut content of the nuts remaining in the bag after I have eaten the almonds?

blocks.text: The minimum almond fraction is 20%, so eating all almonds removes 50 g from 250 g and leaves 200 g. Peanuts can originally be at most 40% of 250 g, or 100 g. That maximum is compatible with the other ingredient ranges, for example 20% almonds, 40% peanuts, 15% brazils, 10% hazelnuts and 15% pecans. The remaining peanut fraction is 100/200=50%, C.

items.label: A
items.text: 40% is the maximum original peanut percentage; removing almonds reduces the denominator and increases that fraction.

items.label: B
items.text: 48% would be 96 g of peanuts out of 200 g. The permitted 100 g gives a larger fraction.

items.label: D
items.text: 57% of the remaining 200 g would require 114 g of peanuts, exceeding the original 100 g maximum.

items.label: E
items.text: 60% would require 120 g, also above the permitted peanut mass.
